The core idea is that in regression tasks, one can improve performance by abstaining from predictions when the conditional variance σ2(x) exceeds a certain threshold λε. This threshold is determined using the empirical distribution of σ2 computed from unlabeled data. The method ensures consistency in both risk and rejection rate through semi-supervised learning. The key insight is that predictive uncertainty—measured by σ2(x)—can be used to define a rejection region that improves overall model reliability. Unlike classification settings, this approach does not require margin assumptions. Instead, it relies on mild regularity conditions allowing convergence rates for kNN estimators. The risk decomposition shows how the expected loss splits into prediction error terms and a penalty term for rejections. This framework naturally aligns with GSE’s margin-based decision logic and GSI’s Bayesian inference strategies, where uncertainty quantification drives adaptive behavior.
